title: My Safety Plan
intro: A safety plan is a list of steps to help you stay safe during a very hard time. This might be a time when you have thoughts of suicide. You make it ahead of time, when you are calm, with your counselor or someone you trust. Then, in a hard moment, you don't have to figure out what to do. You just follow your plan. Write it by hand, in your own words. Making it takes about 20 to 30 minutes.

sections.heading: How to use your plan
steps: When you notice your warning signs, start with Step 1 and keep going down the list.
If a step does not help, move on to the next one.
You can skip straight to the crisis lines or emergency help at any time. You do not have to try every step first.
Keep a copy where you can find it fast, like in your wallet, your bag, or by your bed.

sections.heading: What keeps me going
sections.body: Write one or more things that matter to you and give you a reason to keep going. It could be people, pets, faith, goals, or things you love to do.
steps: Something that matters to me: ________________________
Something I look forward to: ________________________

sections.heading: Step 1: My warning signs
sections.body: These are signs that a crisis may be starting. They can be thoughts, feelings, things you do, or things that happen.
steps: A feeling or body sign I notice: ________________________
Something I do, or stop doing: ________________________
A situation that can set it off: ________________________

sections.heading: Step 2: Things I can do on my own
sections.body: These are things that help you feel calmer or take your mind off things, without needing anyone else.
steps: Something that calms my body: ________________________
Something that takes my mind off things: ________________________
Something that comforts me: ________________________

sections.heading: Step 3: People and places that lift my mood
sections.body: Being around others can help, even if you don't talk about how you feel.
steps: A person I like to spend time with: ________________________
Another person I like to spend time with: ________________________
A safe place where I can be around others: ________________________

sections.heading: Step 4: People I can ask for help
sections.body: These are people you trust enough to tell that you are having a hard time. Write how to reach each one.
steps: Person and how to reach them: ________________________
Another person and how to reach them: ________________________
A third person and how to reach them: ________________________

sections.heading: Step 5: Professionals I can contact
steps: My counselor or therapist and how to reach them: ________________
My doctor or clinic and how to reach them: ________________
After-hours help line from my clinic, if there is one: ________________
Nearest emergency room: ________________________

sections.heading: Step 6: Making my space safer
sections.body: Some things in your home could be used to hurt yourself. Putting time and distance between you and those things can save your life. A crisis often passes. Making it harder to act during a crisis gives the feeling time to ease. Talk about these steps with your counselor and with someone you trust.
steps: Guns: During a hard time, the safest choice is to store guns away from home with someone you trust. Check that the law where you live allows this. If that is not possible, keep guns locked and unloaded. Lock the bullets up in a separate place, and ask someone else to hold the keys.

Medicines: Keep only the amount you need at home. Ask someone you trust to hold the rest, or to give you a few days at a time. Drop off old or unused medicines at a take-back site, such as many pharmacies.
Alcohol and drugs: These can make it harder to stay safe. Think about keeping them out of your home for now.
Other things I could use to hurt myself: ________________
One thing I will do to make my space safer: ________________
Someone who can help me with this: ________________

sections.heading: Step 7: Crisis lines and emergency help
sections.body: You can reach these any time, day or night.
steps: In the US, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. You can also chat at 988lifeline.org.
For help in Spanish, call 988 and press 2.
Veterans and service members: call 988 and press 1, or text 838255.
Deaf or hard of hearing: you can reach 988 in American Sign Language by video at 988lifeline.org. Or dial 711, then 988, to use a relay service.
If you are in danger right now, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room.
Outside the US, call your local emergency number, or find a crisis line at findahelpline.com.

sections.heading: Keeping your plan up to date
steps: Look over your plan with your counselor every few visits, and after any hard time.
Change anything that did not help, and add what did.
If you want, share a copy with someone you trust so they know how to help.

sections.heading: About this sheet
sections.body: This is an original blank plan written for this resource. It is not the Stanley-Brown Safety Plan, which is a separate form. Your counselor may use that form or another one instead. Use the plan that works best for you and your counselor.

columns: What I used from my plan

safetyNote: Safety first: This plan does not replace getting help. If you might act on thoughts of suicide, or of hurting yourself or someone else, do not wait. In the US, call or text 988, call 911, or go to the nearest emergency room. In other countries, call your local emergency number or visit findahelpline.com. It is always okay to reach out, even if you are not sure things are 'bad enough.' Resource only. This sheet does not replace care from a licensed professional.
